title: Should Finance Fund AI Tools or Fix Legacy Systems First? The Copper Line Problem
summary: The FAA and Microsoft 365 outages show how new tech fails on old layers. Why finance should fund its data foundation before more AI in the FY27 budget.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


Abacum's CEO argues that if the FY27 budget forces a choice, finance should fund its data foundation before new AI tools. Abacum, the AI-native business planning platform, sees the pattern the November 2026 FAA and Microsoft 365 outages exposed: new technology failing on older layers. Deloitte found 46% of large-company finance leaders plan to modernize core ERP or unify finance data.


Source:[Deloitte, Finance Trends 2027](https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/insights/topics/leadership/finance-trends-leadership.html) . Survey of 1,434 CFOs and next-in-line finance leaders in 26 countries, spring 2026, companies with revenue of at least $1B.


## Two outages in one week


On Friday afternoon, November 13, the FAA stopped departures at every airport in the country. It lasted more than four hours.


That evening, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the FAA’s aging network. “It is the old hardware that went down,” he said. Over the weekend[his account got more specific](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/15/nx-s1-6041091/duffy-says-work-by-a-contractor-to-upgrade-old-copper-wires-led-to-the-groundstop) . A contractor was swapping a stretch of old copper wire in Arkansas for fiber. Officials say a new router installed in that work started sending thousands of inquiries every few seconds, and the older parts of the network couldn’t take it. Investigators still haven’t confirmed the root cause, but that version is the one worth sitting with.


The day before, Microsoft 365 went down. Outlook, Teams, Copilot, and for some customers it stayed down into the next day.[Microsoft said](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/microsoft/massive-microsoft-365-outage-disrupts-outlook-teams-copilot-worldwide/) “the incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change.”


Two very different failures in the same week. In one, a new part sent an old system more traffic than it was built for. In the other, an upgrade sat on top of an upgrade until one change exposed something nobody knew was there. I think both are coming for finance.


## The copper line problem


Every finance stack I see has a copper line somewhere. It’s the ERP export someone built in 2021 that runs every month and nobody touches. It’s the planning model where adding a dimension means a week of rebuilding. It’s the mapping table that one person on the team understands, and that person is on holiday in December. Right?


None of these are broken. That’s the problem. They work fine at the load they were designed for: a monthly close, a quarterly reforecast, a few people asking a few questions.


Now look at what we are asking them to carry in 2027. With AI, the questions come all day. An agent reads whatever is there, right now, and acts on it. Your budget owners are going to ask Claude or ChatGPT how much budget they have left, and they’ll expect the answer in seconds, from the real numbers. That’s a different load. Totally different load.


So when I hear a plan that is basically “add AI on top of what we have,” I think about that router in Arkansas. Whatever investigators find, the part that fell over in Duffy’s telling was the old network underneath, carrying traffic it was never built for.


Then there is the Microsoft version. Here nothing is old. The problem is upgrade on top of upgrade on top of upgrade. Each one works and each one passes the test, and somewhere in the stack is a decision someone made three versions ago, waiting for the change that exposes it. In finance this shows up as a number on a board slide that nobody can trace. Who changed the driver? Which version of the headcount file? Was it the AI or the analyst?


In finance, “mostly right” is not good enough. When the system can’t explain the number, the CFO has to.


## Fund the foundation first


That’s why the Deloitte number stays with me. These are companies with more AI budget than almost anyone, and nearly half of them are spending FY27 money on the ERP and the data layer. They aren’t doing it because it’s exciting. They’re doing it because they already found out what the AI stands on.


For a lot of you, the FY27 plan locks in the next few weeks. So the decision is real and it’s now: does the money go to new AI capabilities, or to the systems those capabilities will run on? My view is simple. If you have to pick, fund the foundation first. The AI is going to get better every quarter whatever you do. Your copper line is not.


Before you sign the plan, ask your team:


-


Where does our AI actually read the data from, and how old is the data by the time it gets there?


-


How many hops are there between the ERP and the answer on the screen?


-


If questions to our data multiplied overnight, what breaks first?


-


When a number is wrong, can we see who or what changed it?


If the answers make you uncomfortable, that’s your 2027 priority. Not the next pilot. If you’re weighing specific AI budget requests this cycle,[here’s how to decide which ones to approve](https://www.abacum.ai/blog/how-to-approve-ai-budget-requests) .
